profile.reading:
This building is one of Microsoft's Bexar County, Texas data center facilities, though the OSM data underlying this registry entry does not include a specific street address, only the county. Microsoft has built at least eight data centers across the San Antonio region, spanning Bexar and Medina counties, since first opening two facilities there in 2015 at roughly $90 million each; the San Antonio Report reported cumulative Microsoft investment in the region exceeded $1.2 billion as of August 2023. San Antonio's city council approved a 15-year Chapter 380 tax reimbursement in 2013 covering 40% of property taxes in exchange for a $250 million Microsoft investment commitment and the creation of 20 high-paying jobs, an incentive arrangement that has drawn continued local scrutiny as Microsoft has kept expanding well beyond the original commitment. Construction phases at Microsoft's San Antonio campuses have typically employed several hundred workers, while each completed data center building tends to run with a comparatively small operating staff of roughly 50 employees once online. Named Microsoft projects reported in San Antonio include SAT40 in Texas Research Park (about $175.9 million on 70 acres), SAT14 on Wiseman Boulevard (a 411,000-square-foot complex), and the SAT80 pair near Castroville in Medina County (each exceeding 106,000 square feet on a shared 206-acre rural site), but Microsoft has not published which specific building corresponds to this OSM-mapped structure, nor its address, square footage, or MW capacity beyond the county-level location already on record.

CPS Energy, San Antonio's municipally owned electric and gas utility, the largest such public utility in the country, supplies power to Microsoft's San Antonio-area campuses and has cited large commercial and industrial customers, data centers among them, in its own integrated resource planning as it weighs new generation to meet growing demand. Because CPS Energy is municipally owned rather than investor-owned, large-load agreements with customers like Microsoft are negotiated directly with the city-owned utility rather than through the Public Utility Commission of Texas process that governs most of the state's investor-owned utilities.

reading.body:
Microsoft has built at least eight data centers across Bexar and Medina counties since 2015, with cumulative investment exceeding $1.2 billion as of August 2023. This specific facility, TRP1, is one of those campuses, but Microsoft has not published its megawatt capacity, square footage, or which named project it corresponds to. The site sits in Bexar County and draws power from CPS Energy, a municipally owned utility that negotiates large-load agreements directly with the city rather than through the state's investor-owned utility regulator.

Among Texas data centers with published megawatt figures, this facility does not appear, ranking outside the top eighteen published capacities in the state. Of 133 mapped data center facilities in Texas, only eighteen have operator-disclosed power specs, totaling 468 MW. Without TRP1's published capacity, its scale relative to other Texas campuses cannot be determined.

CPS Energy has identified data centers as a material factor in its resource planning as it plans new generation to meet growing regional demand. The utility's municipal ownership means Microsoft's power requirements shape that planning through direct negotiation with the city rather than through Public Utility Commission proceedings. Whether TRP1 represents new capacity or an expansion of an existing named project, its contribution to that demand is not separately disclosed.
